title: A Cricket Behind a Wide Chimney
description: A chimney wider than about 30 inches needs a cricket on the uphill side. Step flashing alone lets Houston rain sit against the brick and find the mortar.
html:
Water running down a roof hits the back of a chimney and has to go somewhere. On a narrow chimney it splits and runs to the sides. On a wide one it stalls, soaks the brick, and finds the joint between the flashing and the mortar. The piece that splits that water is a cricket, a small saddle built on the uphill face.

When the saddle is part of the job

The usual line is 30 inches. If the chimney is wider than that, measured parallel to the ridge, and it does not sit on the ridge itself, we build a cricket. Some older Houston houses never had one. The leak shows up as a stain on the ceiling just downhill of the chimney, or as efflorescence on the brick, white salt where water has been leaving the masonry for years.

Step flashing still belongs on the sides. An apron still belongs on the downhill face. Counterflashing should be cut into the mortar joints, not glued to the face of the brick. A cricket does not replace those. It gives them less water to survive. Caulk smeared where the counterflashing should be regletted is the repair that fails the next time the brick gets hot and the sealant shrinks.

Brick, cap, and the crown

A perfect cricket will not save a chimney crown that is cracked open or a cap that dumps rain straight down the flue chase. We look at those while we are up there. If the masonry is the leak, a mason owns that part. We own the roof side: saddle, step, apron, and a counterflashing that can come off and go back when the roof is replaced later.

If your stain sits on the chimney side of the room, do not start with paint. A roof inspection from the uphill side of the brick tells you whether you need a cricket, a reflashed joint, or both. Request a free inspection or call (281) 541-0027.
